newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Riksbank cuts rate corridor, trims repo rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Riksbank cuts rate corridor, trims repo rate.

text.p: Sweden's Riksbank as expected cut its deposit and lending rates by 50 basis points on Thursday but surprised markets by announcing a 25-basis point cut in its key repo rate to take effect next Tuesday.

With the rate of inflation in Sweden falling to 0.2 percent, its lowest level in four decades, the Riksbank has had free hands to pursue an aggressive monetary policy to stimulate the country's fragile economy.

Thursday's move brought the deposit rate down to 4.25 percent and the lending rate to 5.75 percent, leaving room for more cuts in the repo rate, the central element of the central bank's three-tiered rate corridor.
Reductions in the repo rate are usually announced at the Riksbank's weekly reverse repurchase tenders, which are used to control the money supply on the financial markets.

But Riksbank governor Urban Backstrom took the unprecedented step of setting the rate for next Tuesday's reverse repurchase tender at 4.60 percent, a 25-basis point reduction on the current level of 4.85 percent.
This rate will also apply at the following three repo tenders on November 5, November 12 and November 19.
The repo rate been cut 22 times this year, and has fallen by over four percentage points from its January level of 8.91 percent.
In a statement, the Riksbank said the spectre of high inflation was unlikely to return in the near future.
"The decisions are based on the assessment that the outlook for inflation in the coming years remains in line with the (two percent) inflation target," the bank said.
"The future monetary stance will depend on new information and how it relates to the analysis in the Riksbank's latest (September) inflation report."
Although the lowering of the rate corridor was unanimously tipped by analysts, the decision to cut the repo rate sent a positive ripple of surprise through the market.

"This is quite surprising. The most optimistic view was maybe for a 10 basis point (repo rate) cut. Initial reactions will be very positive, especially at the long end," analyst Per Wolmer Petersen of Den Danske Bank told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

Petersen's predictions were soon fulfilled. The six-month T-bill rate fell nine basis points on the news to 4.47 percent, whilst the yield on the nine-year government bond dipped seven basis points to 7.17 percent.

Other analysts said the move was logical in the light of recent comments by deputy Riksbank governor Lars Heikensten that monetary policy should not be expected to conform to a pre-determined pattern.
Keith Edmonds, analyst at the London-based IBJ, told RFTV this did not necessarily mean the end of the Riksbank's rate-cutting campaign.

"It was certainly more than expected, but I think there is probably more to come. I think they are now moving policy much more in line with the practice we are seeing in other European countries," he said.
